Digital Water Infrastructure

Water moves as one connected system. Our information does not.

Reservoirs, pipes, pumps, fields and factories share the same water cycle — but rarely the same information. We are building the intelligence layer that connects them.

We help operators measure, monitor and manage water systems — with dashboards, remote controls and automation, from a single site to connected networks.

Water Forever is an initiative led by Waterfall Automation Pvt. Ltd., the technology team developing Waterfall Grid.

See the Waterfall GridExplore applications

Make water manageable.

Coordinate people, schedules, pumps and valves; verify the result and expand intelligently.

The idea

Three layers, one grid

Physical water systems stay as they are. We add a digital foundation that connects them, and an intelligence layer that turns the data into decisions.

How the layers fit
Why now

Water can finally be understood as a whole.

Wider connectivity, better sensing, satellite observations and computational tools now make it possible to understand water systems together, at a time of growing uncertainty around availability and demand.

Waterfall Grid

The intelligence layer for water.

Water data in. Situational awareness, operational decisions and verifiable action out. Start by connecting the assets you already have.

Connect → Identify → Understand → Control → Verify.

Explore applications
Imagine a water tank that frequently overflows after dark.

A level reading reveals the pattern. The grid relates it to pump runtime and demand, alerts the operator, and — where authorised — changes pump operation. The next day’s data confirms whether overflow reduced. The same sequence can begin with a village, a construction site, or an industrial plant.

Built on field operations. Waterfall Automation's SICCA sensing, connectivity and pump/valve automation provide a practical engineering foundation. Waterfall Grid extends this foundation towards a shared intelligence layer across different water environments.

6.1.1 · Built Environment

The supervisor’s time is the hidden cost of site water.

Curing, drinking and worker water run as three separate systems on one site. One connected layer lets a supervisor see and operate them without climbing every floor.

Discuss construction water operationsThe Waterfall Grid
One site. Three water systems.

Construction, drinking and worker-domestic water each have different priorities. A unified operations view reduces manual rounds and helps protect pressure for the floors that need it.

Today
  • A supervisor repeatedly inspects and operates pumps, floors, valves and pressure by hand.
  • Curing water competes with other site activity; pressure is uneven where curing is under way.
  • Tanker orders are placed without a clear view of source and storage levels.
With a connected layer
  • Floor-wise remote isolation and schedules for curing water.
  • Source and storage visibility, so tanker orders follow real levels.
  • Monitored tap schedules and abnormal-flow cut-off for worker water.
Who gains
  • Site supervisors
  • Site engineers
  • Project directors
  • Camp managers
  • Procurement

6.1.2 · Built Environment

Design metering into the building. Don’t just add more meters.

Plan the metering topology at MEP stage, so the building has a digital water layer from day one and no duplicated meter points.

Plan my building water architectureThe Waterfall Grid
Better architecture, not more meters.

The useful metering points are decided from source, storage, branches, users and facilities — ideally while the MEP design is still flexible.

Today
  • Meters are added after the plumbing is fixed, without studying the topology.
  • Duplicated points raise capex without adding visibility.
  • Residents, operators and developers each lack a clear view of consumption.
With a connected layer
  • Metering points designed with the water topology at MEP stage.
  • Potentially fewer unnecessary meter points, where the design allows.
  • Resident, building-operator and developer dashboards, by role.
Who gains
  • Residents
  • Building managers
  • Developers
  • MEP consultants

6.1.3 · Built Environment

Premium spaces cannot depend on manual routines.

Irrigation, pumps, lighting and water features run as one controlled system, so a landscape stays healthy and the property experience stays premium.

Explore landscape automationThe Waterfall Grid
The experience depends on the operations.

Automated irrigation, fountains, lighting and pump routines can protect landscape quality without constant manual attention.

Today
  • Over- and under-watering; dry patches beside waterlogged ones.
  • Lighting and pumps depend on staff who must be present at the right time.
  • Pumps can run without real-time protection until a failure is noticed.
With a connected layer
  • Timer-based operation by zone, with selectable days, start times and durations.
  • Short, scheduled irrigation cycles by zone.
  • Pump protection and rotation; scheduled outdoor lighting.
  • Water features and fountains on automated schedules.
Who gains
  • Facility managers
  • Developers
  • Residents and visitors
  • Maintenance teams

6.2.1 · Manufacturing & Industry

Know where every litre goes inside the factory.

Measure water at the boundary and at branch points, understand source-to-use flows, control pumps and valves where it is safe to do so, and keep auditable records, in any manufacturing sector.

Assess my plant water systemThe Waterfall Grid
Account for every direction of flow.

Start at the incoming boundaries. Follow major branches, process consumption, cooling, reuse and outflows to find where measurement and control matter most.

Today
  • Readings are taken by hand on rounds.
  • Section-wise consumption is unclear until month-end.
  • Allocation overruns and abnormal flow are caught late.
With a connected layer
  • Accurate measurement at the boundary and at branch and usage points.
  • Section-wise and process-wise consumption.
  • Daily or shift allocation with auto cut-off where safe.
Who gains
  • Plant operations
  • Utility managers
  • EHS and sustainability
  • Maintenance
  • Leadership

Independently verified: 42% average water saving in the field.

Crop-specific irrigation scheduling, less manual attendance and less unnecessary pumping, verified by a UNIDO-supported measurement and verification study.

Explore precision irrigationThe Waterfall Grid
Independent evidence from the field.

The UNIDO-supported evaluation across agricultural demonstrations provides measured savings evidence for the underlying sensing and automation approach.

Today
  • Irrigation by habit rather than crop need.
  • Manual attendance at the pump, day and night.
  • Unnecessary pumping wastes water and energy.
With a connected layer
  • Crop-specific irrigation scheduling.
  • Automated pump and valve control.
  • Soil and crop condition monitoring.
Who gains
  • Farmers
  • Farm managers
  • Programme funders
  • Researchers

6.4.1 · Public Water Systems

From reservoir to neighbourhood, one operational picture.

Source, treatment, pumping, storage and pipelines are managed in parts. A connected layer can start with existing SCADA and records and add sensors only where gaps remain.

Discuss an urban water networkThe Waterfall Grid
Start with the network already in place.

Connect existing SCADA, logs and meters first. Add focused sensing and control only where operational visibility is missing.

Today
  • Source, plant, pumping and network data sit in different systems.
  • Operators learn of problems late, after complaints.
  • Planning relies on partial, delayed information.
With a connected layer
  • Integrate existing SCADA and records first.
  • Add targeted sensors only where data gaps remain.
  • Flow, pressure, tank-level and pump views in one place.
Who gains
  • Utility operators
  • Plant managers
  • City leadership
  • Planners

6.4.3 · Public Water Systems

Not just the water level. The decision lead time.

Current availability, effective capacity and trends, water movement and environment, then trajectory and preparedness.

Explore reservoir intelligenceThe Waterfall Grid
A level is only one signal.

Availability, rainfall, inflows, releases, evaporation and demand together can improve the time available to prepare.

Today
  • Level is reported without effective capacity or trend.
  • Inflow, outflow, rainfall and evaporation sit in separate records.
  • Dependent villages and farms are not linked to the source.
With a connected layer
  • Availability → effective capacity and history → movement and environment → trajectory.
  • State → district → reservoir drill-down.
  • Inflow, outflow, rainfall and satellite layers with provenance and timestamps.
Who gains
  • District administration
  • Reservoir managers
  • Water departments
  • Researchers

Our Journey › Our Story
Our story

From field-level water automation to a connected understanding of water.

From a field problem to a shared water vision

We began by helping farmers use water more precisely. Building connected sensing and automation in the field led us to villages, buildings and larger networks — where the same missing connection kept appearing: the infrastructure exists, but its information remains fragmented.

Water Forever represents the bigger mission. Waterfall Grid is the intelligence layer we are building to make water systems more measurable, understandable and manageable across sectors.

Read the full founding story

How it began

Our journey began with a practical challenge: helping farmers irrigate with greater precision. Working in the field taught us that water management was not just a question of pumps, pipes or schedules. It was a question of knowing what was happening, understanding what was needed and acting at the right time. We built sensing, connectivity and automation systems to help make that possible.

The realization

As our work expanded into rural drinking-water systems, buildings, construction environments and larger water networks, a common problem became clear. Water itself is connected: it moves through sources, reservoirs, pumps, storage, distribution systems and users. The information surrounding it rarely moves together. It is scattered across instruments, records, departments, operators and applications.

What we are building

Water Forever grew from the belief that this fragmented information should become a connected, trusted foundation for better water decisions. Waterfall Grid is the platform vision: bringing together measurements, existing operational systems, satellite and environmental intelligence, and relevant records, then turning them into context, insights and action where appropriate. We begin with real infrastructure and expand progressively: one system, one site, one network at a time.

Why now

Water infrastructure has existed for generations. Today, wider connectivity, better sensing, satellite observations and computational tools make it increasingly possible to understand these systems together. At a time of growing uncertainty around water availability and demand, the opportunity to turn fragmented information into timely intelligence matters more than ever.

Waterfall Automation Pvt. Ltd. builds and deploys the technology; Water Forever expresses the long-term mission; Waterfall Grid is the platform being developed towards that mission.

FROM ONE VILLAGE TO A DISTRICT

Rajegaon → Jalna

Our field journey now includes a connected village distribution demonstration. Further surveyed villages show how diverse water arrangements can be brought into a common approach, with district intelligence as the next horizon.

From the field

Rajegaon, Jalna district

Connecting village water-distribution components, including pumping, storage and valves, shows how practical monitoring and remote operation can reduce dependence on manual coordination. The next ambition is broader: connect information from villages, reservoirs, distribution networks and water users into a district-level understanding of availability, movement, demand and risk. Rajegaon is the field experience; district intelligence is where we are headed.

Rural distributionDistrict intelligence
Proof that begins in the field
  • Six agricultural demonstration sites across seven crops formed part of an independent CII-Godrej GBC measurement-and-verification exercise under the UNIDO/BEE FLCTD programme.
  • The report documented an average 42% reduction in irrigation water use across the crop demonstrations.
  • Rajegaon provides a separate field example in rural drinking-water distribution; eleven additional interested villages were surveyed for potential expansion.

Read the complete Founder’s Note
A note from the founder
“Water moves as one connected system. Our information does not.”

When I began working with farmers, my objective was relatively simple: help them use water more efficiently. We developed technology that could measure conditions in the field, understand irrigation requirements and automate the delivery of water. But as our work expanded across farms, villages and larger water systems, I began to recognize something more fundamental. A farmer may not know how much water will be available next month. A village operator may struggle to coordinate pumps, storage and distribution. A city, industry or district administration may have large amounts of data, yet lack a connected understanding of what is happening across its water infrastructure. The problem is not always the absence of infrastructure or information. Very often, it is the absence of intelligence connecting them.

That realization became the foundation of Water Forever. I believe the next major step in water management is to build digital infrastructure that allows existing systems to become measurable, connected, interoperable and increasingly intelligent. Through Waterfall Grid, we are working towards an intelligence layer that can bring together sensors, operational systems, public records, satellite observations, environmental information and human expertise, helping us understand not only how much water we have, but where it is moving, how it is being used, what may happen next and what we can do about it. We are starting with practical problems and real infrastructure because lasting transformation must begin on the ground. But the ambition extends beyond any one product, sector, organization or geography.

Water Forever is ultimately about responsibility across generations. Every generation inherits water systems built and managed by those before it. I believe ours has an opportunity, and a responsibility, to make those systems more intelligent, accountable and resilient for those who will come after us. Technology makes this possible; collaboration makes it meaningful. Commercial sustainability gives us the means to continue building. But the purpose is larger: to help ensure that the water humanity depends upon remains available, understood and responsibly managed for generations to come.

Jasveer Singh
Founder, Water Forever · Founder & CEO, Waterfall Automation Pvt. Ltd.
M.Tech (Electronics), IIT Bombay

Jasveer Singh

Founder, Water Forever · Founder & CEO, Waterfall Automation Pvt. Ltd.

Jasveer Singh is an electronics engineer and entrepreneur with an M.Tech from IIT Bombay. He founded Waterfall Automation after years of working at the intersection of sensing, connectivity, automation and practical water-management challenges.

Dr. Manmeet Singh

Scientific Collaborator · AI & Climate Intelligence

Dr. Manmeet Singh is a climate scientist and artificial intelligence researcher with a Ph.D. in Climate Studies from IIT Bombay. He is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Earth, Environmental, and Atmospheric Sciences at Western Kentucky University and Director of its DSOC AI Laboratory.

Read more

A former scientist at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune, and a Fulbright-Kalam Fellow who conducted research at the University of Texas at Austin, his work spans Earth system modelling, AI-supported weather prediction, climate and disaster intelligence, and geospatial analysis. His discussions and collaboration around Waterfall Grid contribute a scientific perspective to reservoir intelligence, satellite data, climate context and the longer-term challenge of turning observations into useful water-system decisions.

What the field has taught us
  • Construction water management also consumes supervisory time; remote control can reduce repeated visits to different floors and equipment.
  • Smart building water intelligence begins with good metering and plumbing architecture, not simply the maximum possible meter count.
  • Village water networks differ widely in sources, distances, storage assets and operating constraints; flexible control matters.
  • The value of individual measurements grows when storage, pumping, distribution, demand and context can be understood together.
